generated_by: prism-parity:tools/generate-agent-responses.php for php; the ports' own runners for ts and py. Every row is execution output from the real client against a stubbed transport — a hand-authored parse result would assert the author's model of the parser.
scope: Parse one Agent API response through retrieve (legacy default), cancel, or create. Cancellation-only response_id presence, exact requested-ID binding, cancelling classification and optional incomplete_details.reason projection are covered. Bounded polling is tested in each client package, not by this single-response corpus.

inputs.http_status: The HTTP status the transport returns.
inputs.body: The raw response body, verbatim. This is UNTRUSTED input: it is whatever the provider sent, and the malformed rows are not hypothetical shapes but the ones a parser is most likely to disagree about.
inputs.operation: Optional retrieve, cancel, or create. Defaults to retrieve for the unchanged legacy rows; cancel uses the fixed requested ID resp_probe.
inputs.project_incomplete_reason: Project the native incompleteReason()/incomplete_reason() result only when true; legacy projections remain unchanged.

cases.title: a completed run with one citation
cases.notes: The control. If this row disagrees the parse is wrong at the top and every other row is noise.

cases.title: a queued run is NOT finished
cases.notes: The value the polling loop turns on. A language that called this terminal would return an empty answer as though it were the final one.

cases.title: an in-progress run is NOT finished
cases.notes: The other non-terminal state, and the one a run spends most of its life in.

cases.title: a failed run is finished, and carries its error as a VALUE
cases.notes: A 200 whose body reports a failed run. The run finished; it just finished badly. Turning this into an exception would lose the id, the usage and the partial output the caller may still want.

cases.title: a cancelled run is finished
cases.notes: Terminal. A poller that kept waiting on this would spin until its attempt budget ran out and then report a timeout for a run that ended promptly.

cases.title: an incomplete run is finished
cases.notes: The least obvious terminal state — it reads like a synonym for in_progress and is not one.

cases.title: a status none of the three languages knows
cases.notes: Perplexity adding a state is a WHEN, not an if. Refusing is the safe answer — a parser that guessed terminal would truncate a live run, and one that guessed non-terminal would poll a finished one to timeout. What matters cross-language is that all three refuse it the SAME way, because the caller switches on the refusal.

cases.title: a response with no id
cases.notes: The id is the handle for retrieve and cancel. A response without one cannot be followed up, so accepting it hands the caller something it cannot act on.

cases.title: a response whose id is the empty string
cases.notes: Falsy in all three languages and present in none of the obvious ways. An empty id passed to retrieve builds a URL for a different endpoint entirely.

cases.title: an HTTP 400 that names its error
cases.notes: The shape prism#31 produced in production. The provider's own error type has to survive into the refusal, or a consumer cannot tell a bad request from a rate limit.

cases.title: an HTTP 500 with no error object at all
cases.notes: A failure the provider did not describe. The fallback identifier is the whole contract here, and it is exactly the sort of string three languages invent separately.

cases.title: a 200 whose body is a JSON array, not an object
cases.notes: A proxy, a captive portal or a misrouted endpoint returns this. Indexing it as a map yields nulls rather than an error, so a parser that does not check the shape reports a missing status instead of an unreadable body.

cases.title: output carrying an element that is not an object
cases.notes: Untrusted structure inside a well-formed envelope. The bare string must not become an output item, and it must not stop the sibling that follows it from being read.

cases.title: citations spread across two output items and two content parts
cases.notes: Citations are flattened out of a three-level nest, and ORDER is the whole value: a UI numbers them and the answer text refers to them by that number. A language that flattened depth-first differently renumbers every citation in the answer.

cases.title: an annotation that is not an object
cases.notes: A citation list is rendered as links. A bare string surviving into it is a value the UI will try to read fields off, and the one that follows it must still arrive.

cases.title: created_at as a numeric STRING
cases.notes: JSON has one number type and providers still send timestamps as strings. Whether this is read, refused or silently nulled is a per-language coercion habit, and the three habits differ more than anything else in this file.

cases.title: a completed run with no output and no sources
cases.notes: A legitimate answer, not a failure — the package's own docs say an empty source list on a completed run is normal. Pinned so no language starts treating emptiness as an error.
